blocks.text: …trust is everything

We have chosen another living being, with an individual mental and emotional world, for a shared stage of life. Consequently, we humans are first and foremost under a constant obligation toward our dog to provide species-appropriate and understanding care.
In most cases, conflicts arise from disregard of species-appropriate handling, misguided expectations and the flawed conclusions and actions resulting from them.
Inner calm, reliability, kindness, compassion and self-assurance – under these conditions our dog sees no reason to come into conflict with us.
What you should know 📋
Acquiring comprehensive knowledge about dogs and their social interactions is the basis for a future free of conflict.
Collecting positive experiences in living together and avoiding negative influences create the basis for harmonious coexistence.
The ability to constantly question and correct our thinking and actions toward our dog in a self-critical way is an indispensable prerequisite for a conflict-free partnership.
The foundation of the relationship 🤝
Trust is the foundation of the relationship between living beings. Any shock leaves damage and cracks that are difficult to heal and can have far-reaching consequences.

The risk of conflict arising is increased in the first months of life, in which the dog has to settle in with us, as well as in the periods of training and imprinting. Mistakes made there out of inexperience can damage the basis of trust lastingly.
Builds trust ✅
Calm and composed communication.
Clear, easy-to-follow movements.
Observing pauses between individual actions.
Praise and affection for all reactions directed toward us.
Taking time for all interactions.
Calm presence and a peaceful state of mind.
Damages trust ⚠️
Hectic and loud handling.
Stressful atmosphere.
Rough behaviour.
Pointless, stressful training procedures.
Physical corrections.
Forced, unfamiliar situations.
Negative influences from us on our dog.
What our dog knows about our expectations 🧠
We humans often suffer from the weakness of directing expectations at the other party. What does our dog know about our expectations and ideas? The answer is simple: The dog knows nothing about them.

In principle, our dog cannot fulfil expectations. He can only do what nature has predisposed him to do – or show learned reaction patterns if we have patiently trained them with him countless times over a long period.

Only then, at the earliest, may we expect the dog to be able to show the desired trained behaviour – provided that our behaviour in the real situation corresponds to our behaviour in the training situation.
What we must bear in mind 📋
We must always reflect on whether we have trained desired courses of action under realistic conditions, reproducibly and often enough that our dog can carry them out routinely.
Safe framework conditions and positive learning successes are the prerequisite – not pressure, not repetition without understanding.
Principle and positive actions ✅

Our actions should always build trust. The ability, with each of our actions, to put ourselves at the same time in the receiving role of the dog and to feel what our action triggers in him is the sole key to avoiding conflicts.

Calm movements – Space-opening gestures – Clear, easy-to-follow sequences – Prolonged stroking – Calm laying on of hands – Sitting and lying together – Early training of carrying and body-inspection handling.
Negative, trust-destroying actions ⚠️
Hectic movements.
Physical reprimands.
Various handling grips for discipline.
Impatient physical interventions.
Physical rank-assertion actions.
We must protect ourselves and our dog from advice that recommends immediate physical submission measures on the dog. The resulting damage can only be repaired with great effort and rarely completely!
How our dog understands us 🗣️

Our dog interprets the emotional colouring and volume of what we say, as well as the sequences of sounds with which we have conditioned desired actions in training. The first factor can reinforce or hinder the second.
Our verbal communication should always be reliable and unambiguously interpretable for our dog. Misunderstandings due to misinterpreted verbal communication are quite common.
Positive ways of communicating ✅
Calm tone of voice.
Short, unambiguous address.
Limited, clear vocabulary.
Praise in play: intense.
Praise in training: warm and calm.
Corrective tone of voice: calm and firm.
A calm, low tone of voice in everyday life creates composure.
Negative ways of communicating ⚠️
Fast, excited speech.
Constantly speaking loudly.
Emotional verbal communication as a basic state.
Shouting at the dog.
Permanently talking at the dog.
Excited or insecure commenting on problematic situations.
Negatively influencing the dog through the situation-dependent emotional colouring of our verbal communication.
Recommended action 💡

Conflicts between our dog and us are situations resulting from misunderstandings and wrong handling, which, when repeated, turn into learned patterns and can then only be corrected with a great deal of effort.
For this reason, when problems arise it is a duty to engage with the dog's nature and to seek advice and support from experienced, level-headed people.
Play 🎾

Play with the dog is essential. Ideal is toys that are easy to grip and durable: leather pieces, firm rolls made of fabric, knotted ropes or balls braided from rope. A sturdy strap or piece of rope should be attached to it so that you can play well with the dog and playfully tug on it together.

The advice that you must not play tug games with the dog in order to avoid aggression can safely be consigned to the realm of fables. Tug games over the toy are completely normal prey games that are necessary for the healthy development of the dog.
Play in the form of throwing away and bringing back serves rather to satisfy the urge to move and the prey drive. The bonding effect between us and our dog is served rather less by this.
Searching 👃

The search for the coveted toy or the food dummy should be made possible several times a day. Searching is the most original way, as a human–dog team, to build bonds and to offer the dog species-appropriate work.
Both in the house and preferably in a natural environment, we hide the dog's favourite object – and he can then search for it joyfully with our support.
The final reward consists of play and the opening of the food dummy, revealing its tasty contents. The search can be repeated as often as desired until our dog is satisfied.
Everyday routines 🏠

We take care not to oversaturate our dog verbally. Permanently talking at the dog is as unpleasant for him as loud, emotionally exaggerated communication. What is pleasant is calm, harmonious and action-oriented communication.

We move calmly and in a balanced way in the presence of the dog. Situations that provoke conflict are to be avoided: We neither leave objects lying around nor leave things within reach that the dog is not supposed to take notice of.
The feeding place should be in an undisturbed area. Permanently bothering the dog at his lying and sleeping place can provoke conflicts – we accept his rest times and resting places.
The home environment should offer surroundings of calm and reliability. The calmer things are in the house, the sooner the dog finds his harmonious basic state.
Every kind of activity is initiated calmly and clearly. At the beginning the dog goes through doors and stairs on the leash and, as a rule, following us.

All actions of the dog that will be undesired in future are trained away exclusively with the help of the leash. Any training of everyday routines is finally praised and brought to a close with calm gestures.
Practical impulse: Trust is built in everyday life

It is not the big training session that decides the trust between you and your dog – it is the hundred small moments of everyday life. The calm tone when you put him on the leash. The pause before you open the door. The relaxed stroking without haste. Each of these gestures is a building block. Start with one today.
→ Do I regularly question my thinking and actions toward my dog in a self-critical way?
→ Is my communication calm, short and unambiguously interpretable for my dog?
→ Do I consistently avoid physical corrections and rank-assertion actions?
→ Do I expect from my dog only what I have trained with him often enough and positively?
→ Do I offer my dog genuine, bonding play with toys every day?
→ Do I make searching possible for my dog several times a day – as species-appropriate work?
→ Is our home environment a place of calm, reliability and freedom from conflict?
→ Do I accept my dog's rest times and resting places without disturbance?
→ Do I initiate all activities calmly, clearly and in a structured way?
→ Trust is built through every single positive interaction – anew every day!
